sections.heading: 00 — README
sections.intro:
**Polymer Ph.D. — Physical Fitness knowledge package**

This folder contains a synthesised knowledge base built from the Georges St-Pierre RUSHFIT home
training program — nine DVD workout sessions (transcribed locally with Whisper; none were ever
captioned or posted to YouTube) and five program guides (a Workout Guide, a Nutrition Guide, and
three 8-week training calendars).

---

sections.heading: What this is
sections.intro:
**This package synthesises one complete home-fitness program**, designed by mixed martial artist
Georges St-Pierre and his trainer Erik Owings. Every claim in it traces back to a specific
source — a timestamp in a workout video, or a page in a guide.

This is the first Polymer Ph.D. library built from local media rather than YouTube: the DVDs have
no public URL, and their transcripts came from local Whisper speech recognition rather than
platform-supplied captions. The `program` facet exists specifically so this library can later
hold other home-fitness programs alongside RUSHFIT, the way `human-performance` holds multiple
YouTube creators under one roof — see each note's frontmatter.

**Nothing in this package originates outside the source transcripts and guides.**

---

sections.heading: What was processed
sections.intro:
| Measure | Figure |
|---|---|
| Sources written up as structured notes | **14** (9 videos, 5 PDF guides) |
| Program | **RUSHFIT** (Georges St-Pierre / Erik Owings) |
| Total video runtime | **~11.7 hours**, transcribed locally (Whisper, `small` model) |
| Knowledge files in this package | **11** (numbered files 00–08 and 10; `09_SOURCE_CATALOG.md` self-regenerates) |

See `09_SOURCE_CATALOG.md` (generated mechanically from the notes, so it is always complete and
current) for the exact source list.

---

sections.heading: How it was built
sections.intro:
The package follows the same two-stage process as this project's other libraries:

**Stage 1 — extraction.** Each video was transcribed locally with Whisper (`scripts/add_local_video.py`,
written for this library since no existing script handled a local, non-YouTube video file) and
each PDF guide extracted page-by-page with `scripts/add_pdf.py`. Every transcript and extraction
was then read once and turned into a structured note preserving central claims, glossary terms,
analogies, the source's own confidence statements, and `[mm:ss]`/`[p.N]` anchors back to the
source.

**Stage 2 — synthesis.** The knowledge files are written **from the notes, never from raw
transcripts.**

That separation is the anti-fabrication mechanism. **If a claim is not in a note, it does not
appear in this package.**

A structural note on this corpus specifically: several DVDs share an identical warm-up and
cool-down sequence verbatim, and three of the nine DVDs close by re-running the entire Foundation
Moves DVD in full. Rather than re-deriving that shared content in every note, later notes describe
it briefly and cross-reference the note that covers it in full — a deliberate choice to avoid
diluting the corpus with duplicate text, not a gap in coverage.

---

sections.heading: The files
sections.intro:
| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| **`00_README.md`** | This file |
| **`01_CORE_PRINCIPLES.md`** | Cross-cutting principles this program returns to, across DVDs and guides |
| **`02_MOVEMENTS_AND_TECHNIQUE.md`** | The foundation movements and their technique cues, as taught across the corpus |
| **`03_PRACTICES_AND_PROTOCOLS.md`** | Workout formats, the RUSHFIT Assessment, nutrition timing, and the training calendars |
| **`04_SIGNALS_AND_SELF_ASSESSMENT.md`** | Form cues, fatigue signals, and modification triggers the sources describe |
| **`05_CROSS_SOURCE_COMPARISON.md`** | Where sources converge, repeat verbatim, or extend each other |
| **`06_OPEN_QUESTIONS.md`** | What this corpus does not cover or leaves unresolved |
| **`07_PLAIN_ENGLISH_GLOSSARY.md`** | Every technical/program-specific term the notes introduce, defined in plain language |
| **`08_QUESTIONS_AND_ANSWERS.md`** | Worked answers in the package's house style |
| **`09_SOURCE_CATALOG.md`** | All sources — ID, title, kind, duration/page count, workouts, exercises. **Generated mechanically from the notes, so it is complete by construction** |
| **`10_CUSTOM_GPT_INSTRUCTIONS.md`** | The system instructions, boundaries, and scope guidance |

*(Only files carrying source-ID citations by design would be `topic_reference_*.md` files —
none exist yet; this is a single-program corpus without the cross-creator depth that motivates
them in libraries like `nutrition` or `human-performance`.)*

---

sections.heading: What the package does not cover
sections.intro:
- **Exercise science evidence.** This corpus is entirely instructional/programmatic — the
  program's own coaching rationale and demonstrations, not cited studies. Nothing here should be
  read as a research citation.
- **Medical or diagnostic advice.** Nothing here substitutes for a physician's evaluation; the
  program's own guides repeatedly say the same.
- **Other home-fitness programs.** This library is architecturally ready to hold them (see the
  `program` facet), but none are ingested yet.
- **Anything outside the source transcripts and guides.** No outside fitness or nutrition theories
  are introduced.

---

sections.heading: Upload guidance
sections.intro:
**These files are made for pasting into a ChatGPT Custom GPT's knowledge base.** Upload the
numbered files together.

**Suggested setting:** turn web browsing **off** — the value of this collection depends on the GPT
answering from this specific program rather than blending in outside fitness advice it can't
attribute.

sections.heading: 01 — Core Principles
sections.intro:
This library holds 14 sources from one program — RUSHFIT — so the patterns below are not
cross-creator convergence the way they would be in a multi-source library; they are principles
the program itself states and restates, often nearly verbatim, across independent DVDs and
guides. That repetition is still worth naming: it marks what the program treats as load-bearing
rather than incidental.

---

subsections.body:
Repeated across more sources than any other single idea: `foundation-moves` ("quality over
quantity... don't try to use a bunch of weight"), the Workout Guide's equipment page ("It's not
how much weight you lift! The secret to the results comes from endurance and the strength built
up by pushing your body through maximum reps — not maximum weight"), `strength-and-endurance`'s
"no magic pill" framing, and `explosive-power-training`'s explicit rep caps (as few as 3-5 reps
per set) specifically to preserve movement quality over volume. The program applies this same
rule to two different training modes — grinding-endurance circuits and explosive plyometrics —
which is what makes it a principle rather than advice tied to one workout style.
subsections.heading: 1. Quality of repetition beats quantity, stated as the program's central rule

subsections.body:
`foundation-moves` states this as a foundational concept before covering any dumbbell movement:
"We have to activate the core before we squat. We don't want to have a loose core because then
everything tumbles in." `abdominal-strength-and-core-conditioning` extends it into a mechanistic
claim about striking power itself — core as "the bridge" between leg drive and knuckle contact.
Nearly every workout note's "Form cues" section independently names a core-activation failure
(hip sag, rounded back, collapsing plank) as the root cause of a specific technical fault, not a
separate issue from it.
subsections.heading: 2. Core activation is the prerequisite to every other movement, not one exercise among many

subsections.body:
Stated explicitly as the program's philosophy in `balance-and-agility`'s closing discussion
("he's not doing it to the point where he feels joint pain... he's pushing to his full potential")
and restated as a formal rule in the Workout Guide ("You should never do anything that is painful
or could cause injury"). Cheating a rep, skipping reps, or falling short of perfect form is
explicitly sanctioned throughout the corpus; a rep that produces pain is not — this distinction is
drawn consistently enough across independent sources to treat as the program's actual safety
standard, distinct from technical perfection.
subsections.heading: 3. The safety line is pain, not imperfect form

subsections.body:
`strength-and-endurance` and `full-body-strength-and-conditioning` both build entire sessions
around GSP naming his own limitation directly: explosive, fast-twitch strength is his comparative
advantage, sustained isometric/endurance work is his admitted weakness. `explosive-power-training`
independently confirms the inverse — Erik calls explosiveness "one of my favorite workouts" for
GSP specifically because it's his strength. The two DVDs read as a matched pair describing the
same athlete's profile from opposite sides, not independent claims.
subsections.heading: 4. Functional training exposes an individual's weak link — and the program uses GSP's own as the example

subsections.body:
Stated independently in `the-fight-conditioning-workout` ("that vertical to horizontal. Going down
and up. It really tires out the body") and `full-body-strength-and-conditioning` ("this is what
makes mixed martial arts so difficult... going horizontal to vertical"). This is the stated design
rationale behind combining striking/standing work with groundwork/takedowns in the same round,
rather than training them in separate sessions.
subsections.heading: 5. The vertical-to-horizontal transition is named as the specific mechanism behind fight fatigue

subsections.body:
Every workout DVD in the corpus opens with the identical Rush Fit Warmup and closes with the
identical stretch sequence, and multiple sources state directly why: the warm-up's value is "the
form... not the repetition" (`balance-and-agility`), and the cool-down is reframed repeatedly as
more than physical — "a way to change my mind... from being the athlete... to the everyday normal
guy" (stated identically across `the-fight-conditioning-workout`, `full-body-strength-and-conditioning`,
`abdominal-strength-and-core-conditioning`, `strength-and-endurance`, and `explosive-power-training`).
subsections.heading: 6. Warm-up and cool-down are treated as load-bearing, not optional bookends

subsections.body:
`stretch-for-flexibility` states this directly as "the yin to the yang" of the harder conditioning
sessions, backed by GSP naming his own cost for neglecting it (a competition adductor injury, and
years of skipped post-workout stretching). This isn't presented as a nice-to-have recovery add-on
but as equally necessary maintenance, with its own dedicated DVD.
subsections.heading: 7. Flexibility work is explicitly framed as necessary counterbalance, not lesser priority

subsections.body:
"You always have one side better than the other. That is normal" appears, in close paraphrase,
across `balance-and-agility`, `stretch-for-flexibility`, and `strength-and-endurance`. Every
workout note documents at least one explicitly sanctioned modification (kneeling, shortened range
of motion, a substituted easier variant) presented as equally legitimate, not a lesser fallback —
this is a consistent structural feature of how the program teaches every movement, not just a
courtesy aside.

---

Every other file in this package applies one or more of these patterns to a specific topic —
technique, protocol structure, or form cues.
subsections.heading: 8. Individual variation is repeatedly named rather than smoothed into one standard

sections.heading: 02 — Movements and Technique
sections.intro:
The corpus teaches its movement vocabulary in one place — `foundation-moves` — then reuses and
occasionally deepens it across the other eight DVDs. This file indexes where each movement is
taught in full and where it's extended; it does not re-derive the technique cues themselves —
see the named note for those, quoted with anchors.

subsections.body:
Taught in full in `foundation-moves`: squat, lunge (four directions), push-up, sit-up, back
extension, rotation, core activation, burpee/squat thrust. Each carries a named common fault and
at least one sanctioned modification (see `04_SIGNALS_AND_SELF_ASSESSMENT.md` for the fault/fix
pairs specifically).

These same movements reappear inside the shared Rush Fit Warmup (`balance-and-agility`,
`stretch-for-flexibility`, `the-fight-conditioning-workout`, `full-body-strength-and-conditioning`,
`abdominal-strength-and-core-conditioning`, `strength-and-endurance`, `explosive-power-training`,
`bonus-workouts`) at a brisker pace with less fault-and-modification detail — `foundation-moves`
is the corpus's only deep technical treatment of them.
subsections.heading: Bodyweight foundation movements

subsections.body:
Also taught in full in `foundation-moves`: addressing the dumbbell, dumbbell squat, dumbbell
lunge, dumbbell standing press, dumbbell row, upright row/high pull, dumbbell power clean,
dumbbell swing, dumbbell get-up. `full-body-strength-and-conditioning`,
`abdominal-strength-and-core-conditioning`, and `strength-and-endurance` each run the entire
`foundation-moves` DVD again in full as their closing segment — the technique content is
identical in all four places.

Two DVDs extend specific dumbbell movements beyond what `foundation-moves` covers:

- **`explosive-power-training`** trains the power clean and push press as *explosive*,
  rep-capped movements rather than the controlled, deliberate versions `foundation-moves` teaches
  — same mechanics, different intent (see `01_CORE_PRINCIPLES.md` §1).
- **`strength-and-endurance`** introduces the dumbbell "around the world" (a torso-rotation swing
  not covered in `foundation-moves`) and the half get-up as a standalone core movement tied
  explicitly to the "hip heist" fight application.
subsections.heading: Dumbbell foundation movements

subsections.body:
Taught only in `the-fight-conditioning-workout`, in a dedicated closing section that pairs each
technique's real-fight application with its solo workout adaptation: fighting stance, footwork
(forward/back, lateral, pivot), jab, cross, hook, uppercut, rear vertical elbow, front elbow, rear
knee, front kick, roundhouse kick, defensive side kick, checking a kick, level change, sprawl, the
shot/takedown setup, slam, uchi-mata, hip escape, the "hip heist," armbar, kimura, triangle choke,
and the standing guard pass. No other DVD in the corpus covers combat technique directly — the
other eight are body-weight/dumbbell conditioning built from these same movement patterns without
naming the technique they mirror.
subsections.heading: Fight technique (striking, kicks, and grappling)

subsections.body:
The "hip heist" (standing up from beneath an opponent, sourced to GSP's own BJJ vocabulary) is
transcribed three different ways by Whisper in three different notes: "hip eyes"
(`foundation-moves`), "hip-hist"/"hip-high" and "hip ice" (`the-fight-conditioning-workout`), and
correctly-adjacent phrasing in `strength-and-endurance`. Each note preserves its own source
file's literal (garbled) wording rather than silently normalizing to the likely-intended spelling
— see `05_CROSS_SOURCE_COMPARISON.md` for why.
subsections.heading: A term inconsistently auto-transcribed across three sources

subsections.body:
The Workout Guide's "training philosophy" pyramid (`rushfit-workout-guide`) explicitly names
technique — "throw a proper jab, cross, left hook, elbow or knee" — as the *next* tier up from
this conditioning program's own scope, requiring the conditioning base first. The fight-technique
breakdown in `the-fight-conditioning-workout` is the corpus's only source that actually delivers
technique instruction rather than conditioning built from technique-shaped movement patterns.
subsections.heading: The training-camp technique link (from the guides)

subsections.body:
Most conditioning DVDs (`the-fight-conditioning-workout`, `full-body-strength-and-conditioning`,
`abdominal-strength-and-core-conditioning`, `strength-and-endurance`) use **time-boxed,
max-effort rounds**: a fixed window (30-60s, sometimes 2-5 minutes), as many quality reps as
possible, explicitly not capped. `explosive-power-training` uses the opposite format
deliberately: a **hard rep cap** (8 max in round 1, 3-5 max afterward) regardless of remaining
time, because the goal is preserving the stretch-shortening cycle's explosiveness rather than
accumulating fatigue — see `01_CORE_PRINCIPLES.md` §1. Both formats are described as intentional
choices matched to what each session trains, not a stylistic accident.
subsections.heading: Two distinct interval formats, deliberately different

subsections.body:
Four exercises — squat, push-up, sit-up, burpee — each performed for 60 seconds at maximum
effort with a 20-second break between. Introduced conceptually in `rushfit-workout-guide` (with
GSP's own reference scores: 75 squats, 57 push-ups, 55 sit-ups, 22 burpees) and walked through
step-by-step in `bonus-workouts`. Framed explicitly as a repeatable progress-tracking tool, not a
pass/fail test — first-attempt scores below GSP's are named as an expected, normal outcome in
both sources independently.
subsections.heading: The RUSHFIT Fitness Assessment

subsections.body:
A named technique in its own right (`foundation-moves`): set weights on a chair, table, or rack
at knee-to-waist height, and pick them up with a flat, neutral spine rather than bending over a
floor-level weight. GSP names his own occasional violation of this as bad-but-survivable form due
to a strong core, explicitly warning against relying on that same margin ("just because you can
get away with it, you should try not to").
subsections.heading: Addressing the dumbbell

subsections.body:
`rushfit-nutrition-guide` gives a personal-BMR-based calorie target (height/weight/age/gender
formula × an activity multiplier tied to weekly training frequency), then a near-mirror-image
macro swap around training: 65% carbs / 35% protein / 10% fat pre-workout, versus 35% carbs / 55%
protein / 10% fat post-workout. A stated floor (1,200 calories/day minimum) and a stated healthy
pace (1-2 lbs/week) bound the weight-loss guidance on both ends.
subsections.heading: Nutrition timing and macros

subsections.body:
`rushfit-workout-guide` sets a blanket target of 60-80% of max heart rate (220 minus age) for
general training, with a five-zone chart (Zone 1 "healthy heart" 50-60% through Zone 5
"red-line" 90-100%) reproduced identically in all three training calendars for reference.
subsections.heading: Heart-rate training zones

subsections.body:
`rushfit-beginner-training-calendar`, `rushfit-intermediate-training-calendar`, and
`rushfit-advanced-training-calendar` each sequence the same seven DVDs across the same 8 weeks,
with the identical equipment (2-25 lb dumbbells) and the identical midpoint cardio-dosage increase
(30 min → 40+ min at Zone 3). What actually varies between tiers, confirmed by direct comparison:

- **Beginner** has the most built-in rest — 10 rest days across 56, including two extra
  mid-week rest days (11, 31) neither harder tier includes.
- **Intermediate** compresses to a strictly weekly rest cadence (8 rest days) and introduces
  Full Body Strength and Conditioning and Explosive Power Training earlier and more often than
  Beginner.
- **Advanced** keeps Intermediate's weekly rest cadence but adds same-day double sessions
  (AM/PM splits, including two full workout DVDs on some days) — the one calendar in the corpus
  built around session-doubling rather than added frequency alone.

All three point to the RUSHFIT Assessment and the Foundation Moves DVD as prerequisites before
starting the grid itself.
subsections.heading: The three-tier calendar progression

sections.heading: 04 — Signals and Self-Assessment
sections.intro:
Named fault-and-fix pairs, collected from each note's own "Form cues and body signals addressed"
section. Grouped by what the signal indicates, not by which DVD it appears in — several of these
recur nearly verbatim across independent sources (see `05_CROSS_SOURCE_COMPARISON.md`).

subsections.body:
- **Knees buckling inward** during any squat variation — `foundation-moves` calls this "a
  definite no-no," distinct from every other fault in the corpus, which is graded by severity.
- **Looking at the weight during a swing** (risks spinal overextension) — `foundation-moves`,
  `full-body-strength-and-conditioning`.
- **Taking your eyes off the weight during a get-up** (risk of being struck by it) —
  `foundation-moves`, `full-body-strength-and-conditioning`, `strength-and-endurance`.
subsections.heading: Unconditional faults (never acceptable, regardless of fatigue)

subsections.body:
- **Hip sag** (plank, row, lateral plank) → the specific symptom of core fatigue; the fix is
  lifting the hips, not resting — `abdominal-strength-and-core-conditioning`,
  `strength-and-endurance`.
- **Body tilting during a stability hold** → named directly as core fatigue, fixed by widening
  the base, not by trying harder at the same width — `abdominal-strength-and-core-conditioning`.
- **A wobbling, unstable single-leg movement** → add a support point (foot down, brace arm), not
  a sign to abandon the movement — `full-body-strength-and-conditioning`, `balance-and-agility`.
- **Losing balance and needing to step down** → explicitly normalized as "natural and normal,"
  not a failure — `balance-and-agility`, `strength-and-endurance`.
- **A decline in form under fatigue** → expected and acceptable up to the point of "complete
  decay," which is the actual stopping signal — `strength-and-endurance`,
  `bonus-workouts` (RUSHFIT Assessment).
subsections.heading: Fatigue signals that call for a specific, named adjustment (not stopping)

subsections.body:
- **Breath held or restricted during a plank/isometric hold** → "keep everything in place... try
  to breathe into the back of the lungs" — `foundation-moves`.
- **Inability to breathe normally in a stretch position** → the position itself is too
  aggressive; back off — `stretch-for-flexibility`.
- **A specific breathing-under-fatigue cue**: "the body is like a straw. If you bend the straw,
  the air doesn't go through" — stay upright rather than folding over when winded —
  `full-body-strength-and-conditioning`.
subsections.heading: Breathing as a monitored signal, not background

subsections.body:
- **No-discomfort is the stated ceiling for every held stretch**, repeated near-verbatim across
  `stretch-for-flexibility` and `the-fight-conditioning-workout`'s cool-down: "It's not supposed
  to feel any pain... your body will naturally allow you to go a little bit further each time" —
  forcing past that point is named as counterproductive ("you tear muscle and become less
  flexible in the end"), not just risky.
subsections.heading: Stretch/flexibility-specific ceiling

subsections.body:
- **Fixing your gaze on a stationary point** is the corpus's consistent balance cue, stated
  identically in `balance-and-agility` ("if I look this way, I'll fall down... stay looking right
  at your target") and `abdominal-strength-and-core-conditioning`.
subsections.heading: Balance-specific cue

subsections.body:
`rushfit-workout-guide`: "You should never do anything that is painful or could cause injury" —
stated as a formal rule, not an in-workout aside, and the same line every workout DVD's own
closing philosophy discussions independently arrive at (most explicitly in `balance-and-agility`).
subsections.heading: The program's one blanket rule tying all of the above together

sections.heading: 05 — Cross-Source Comparison
sections.intro:
This is a single-program corpus, so "cross-source comparison" here means something different than
in a multi-creator library: not disagreement between independent voices, but how the *same*
production deliberately reuses, extends, or occasionally repeats itself verbatim across nine DVDs
and five guides.

subsections.body:
- **The Rush Fit Warmup** opens all eight workout DVDs (every one except `foundation-moves`
  itself) with identical cueing, down to the same "body is like an elastic" line.
- **The cool-down stretch sequence** closes `the-fight-conditioning-workout`,
  `full-body-strength-and-conditioning`, `abdominal-strength-and-core-conditioning`,
  `strength-and-endurance`, and `explosive-power-training` identically, including the same
  closing "changing my mind" framing word-for-word.
- **`foundation-moves` is re-run in full** as the second half of `full-body-strength-and-conditioning`,
  `abdominal-strength-and-core-conditioning`, and `strength-and-endurance`.
- **`stretch-for-flexibility` and `balance-and-agility` are re-run in full** inside
  `bonus-workouts`, which otherwise contributes only the RUSHFIT Assessment as new content.

This confirms the shared modules are a deliberate production choice (a fixed warm-up/cool-down
module, and closing-DVD "review" pattern), not coincidental overlap between independently written
sessions.
subsections.heading: Verbatim shared modules

subsections.body:
`strength-and-endurance` builds its entire session around GSP naming isometric/endurance work as
his personal weakness ("I'm a more fast-switch muscle-oriented guy... this is my weakness").
`explosive-power-training` independently confirms the inverse from Erik's side: "George has
incredible explosive power. And this is the way you get it, plyometric training. It's one of my
favorite workouts." Neither note cites the other, but read together they describe one consistent
athletic profile.
subsections.heading: The same athlete, described from opposite sides

subsections.body:
GSP's "I'm in pain right now, but I know that's what I need" appears twice in
`full-body-strength-and-conditioning` and in close paraphrase as "the worst day of my life... but
that's what I need" in `bonus-workouts`' RUSHFIT Assessment segment — the same rhetorical move
(naming the pain honestly, then reframing it as purposeful) recurs rather than being confined to
one video.
subsections.heading: A recurring personal catchphrase, not a one-off line

subsections.body:
The "hip heist" (see `02_MOVEMENTS_AND_TECHNIQUE.md`) is auto-transcribed three different ways —
"hip eyes," "hip-hist"/"hip ice," and a third rendering in `strength-and-endurance` — across three
independent DVDs. Each note preserves its own source file's literal wording rather than silently
normalizing to a single "correct" spelling, consistent with this project's rule against importing
terminology the source itself didn't clearly state. The consistent underlying *concept* (standing
up from beneath an opponent via a hip-driven motion) is the same across all three, which is how we
know it's one term garbled three ways rather than three different things.
subsections.heading: A term the corpus can't spell consistently

subsections.body:
`rushfit-workout-guide`'s Personal Information Worksheet points readers to the Nutrition Guide's
BMR calculation, and the Nutrition Guide's own BMR section points back to the Workout Guide's
worksheet to record the result. Each PDF cites the other by page number.
subsections.heading: The Workout Guide and Nutrition Guide are a linked pair, not independent documents

subsections.body:
`foundation-moves` teaches the base version of every bodyweight and dumbbell movement.
`the-fight-conditioning-workout`'s closing technique section is the only source that names the
*fight application* behind movements `foundation-moves` and `strength-and-endurance` teach purely
as conditioning (the get-up as "hip heist," the sprawl/level-change as takedown defense) — later
sources add fight-specific meaning to movements earlier sources already taught mechanically.
subsections.heading: Extension, not repetition: technique depth increases with each pass

subsections.body:
Unlike `dupuytren` or `nutrition`, nothing in this library cites a study, a named researcher, or
an external data source. Every claim is the program's own coaching rationale or GSP's personal
account. This isn't a gap to fix — it accurately reflects what kind of source material this is —
but it means questions like "is this actually the most effective protocol" have no answer this
library can give; it can only report what the program itself claims and how confidently.
subsections.heading: No outside evidence anywhere in this corpus

subsections.body:
All three training calendar PDFs have a page (the heart-rate-zone chart) and the front cover that
extracted no usable text at all — not garbled, simply empty, because those pages are pure
graphics. This library's calendar notes were written from direct visual inspection of the
rendered pages rather than the text layer, and say so explicitly. If those PDFs are ever
re-ingested with OCR tooling, it's worth re-checking whether OCR recovers anything beyond what
was already read directly.

subsections.body:
Only `the-fight-conditioning-workout` names striking/kicking/grappling technique directly by its
real-fight application. The other eight sources teach the same underlying movement patterns
(squat, lunge, level change, sprawl) purely as conditioning, without stating the technique they
mirror — so a reader asking "how is X used in an actual fight" for most named movements will only
find an answer if that movement happens to be one of the ones `the-fight-conditioning-workout`
or `foundation-moves` explicitly ties to a fight application (the get-up/"hip heist" being the
clearest case).
subsections.heading: The fight-technique depth is uneven across the corpus

sections.heading: 07 — Plain English Glossary
sections.intro:
Every program-specific or technical term the notes introduce, defined in plain language.
Alphabetical, no citations — see each note's own "Glossary terms introduced" section for the
sourced version with anchors.

**Addressing the dumbbell** — the technique for approaching and picking up a dumbbell set on an
elevated surface (chair, table, rack height) with a flat, neutral spine, as distinct from the
lift itself.

**Airplane** — a balance exercise: standing on one leg, arms out wide, rotating the torso side to
side.

**Alligator crawl (bear crawl)** — an elbow-to-knee crawl kept as low to the floor as possible;
the lower the hips, the harder it is.

**"Around the world"** — a single-dumbbell exercise that swings the weight in a circle from one
hand to the other, with the heels lifting off the ground.

**Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR)** — the number of calories a body needs in a day, calculated from
height, weight, age, gender, and activity level.

**The calorie equation** — calories burned minus calories eaten equals the calorie deficit that
drives fat loss; a 3,500-calorie deficit equals about one pound of fat.

**Chair iso-squat** — holding a squat at the bottom position without moving, rather than doing
repetitions.

**The "championship round"** — the program's own name for a workout's final, hardest round,
meant to feel like the decisive round of a fight.

**Checking a kick** — a defensive move: raising the leg to block an incoming kick while covering
the face with the other arm.

**Clench-and-relax** — a whole-body relaxation sequence at the end of a workout: tense every
muscle on an inhale, then let go completely on the exhale.

**Closed guard position** — a ground-fighting position (on your back, legs around an opponent)
that some floor exercises are built to simulate.

**Fencer's lunge** — an explosive jumping lunge that alternates which direction you face.

**Floor pull-up with pop-up** — lying face down, pulling yourself forward along the ground with
your elbows, then popping up to standing.

**Ginga** — a Capoeira dance/martial-arts step, moving side to side like a backward lunge with a
raised guard hand.

**Gorilla squat** — hands on the floor like a gorilla, hopping the feet up into a full squat and
standing, then repeating.

**Hip-heist** — standing back up from underneath an opponent using a hip-driven motion; the same
term this program's automatic transcription rendered several different ways ("hip eyes," "hip
ice," "hip-hist") across different videos.

**The low shuffle** — a lateral shuffling drill done in a low stance, said to improve kicking
power.

**"Mawa shigiri"** — almost certainly "mawashi geri," the standard term for a roundhouse kick;
hip-driven, with the heel pointed at the target on impact.

**Mule kick (bullfrog drill)** — hands braced on the floor, kicking both legs up together, then
standing.

**Navasana** — the yoga "boat pose": sitting with legs and chest lifted, forming a V shape.

**The opposites drill** — a stability exercise on all fours or kneeling, lifting the opposite arm
and leg together and holding.

**"The piston"** — this program's name for a dumbbell squat, because the up-and-down motion looks
like a piston.

**Quality over quantity** — the program's repeated rule for adding weight: use only what you can
lift with good form, not as much as possible.

**RUSHFIT Assessment** — a four-exercise fitness test (squat, push-up, sit-up, burpee, one minute
each) used to measure progress before and during the program.

**The scramble** — a fast-paced drill moving between full and half body rotations, supported only
on the hands and feet.

**Sit-through** — a transitional floor movement passing through a push-up-like position on the
way from lying down to standing.

**Staggered butterfly guard / staggered hooks guard** — ground-fighting positions that the
dumbbell get-up's starting posture is said to functionally resemble.

**Straddle** — a wide seated or standing leg position used as the base for several stretches.

**The stretch-shortening cycle** — the mechanism behind explosive (plyometric) training: a muscle
stretched quickly, like a rubber band, snaps back with more force than a muscle moved slowly.

**The training pyramid (Conditioning / Technical / Tactical)** — the program's own three-level
model of athletic development: a base of general fitness (Conditioning), then sport-specific
skills (Technical), then match-specific strategy (Tactical).

**Triple extension** — the simultaneous straightening of the ankle, knee, and hip joints that
powers an Olympic-lift-style jumping motion.

**Uchi-mata** — a judo hip throw, adapted in this program as a defensive response to being grabbed
or clinched.

**The "yin to the yang"** — this program's own phrase for how flexibility work balances out its
harder conditioning work — necessary, not optional.

sections.heading: 08 — Questions and Answers (worked examples)
sections.intro:
These are worked examples of the house style this package's Custom GPT should follow: answer from
the corpus, cite the source note, and say plainly when the corpus doesn't cover something rather
than filling the gap with outside fitness knowledge.

---

**Q: My knees cave in when I squat. Is that a big deal?**

Yes — this is one of the only faults in the entire corpus called out as unconditional rather than
graded by severity. `foundation-moves` states directly: "This is a definite no-no. We want the
knees coming out." The fix offered is widening your stance slightly and going shallower rather
than continuing at full depth with the knees caving.

---

**Q: I can't do a full sit-up without it hurting my back. What do I do?**

Every source that teaches the sit-up offers the same named substitution: an abdominal crunch
(lifting only the shoulder blades off the ground, not the full torso). `foundation-moves` frames
this explicitly as a legitimate variation, not a lesser one: "there's nothing wrong with just
doing an abdominal crunch variation... eventually as you get stronger, work yourself into a full
range of motion."

---

**Q: Why does the program spend a whole DVD on stretching?**

`stretch-for-flexibility` states this directly as the reason: flexibility work is "the yin to the
yang" of the program's harder conditioning sessions — necessary to maintain joint health and
range of motion, not optional recovery. GSP backs this with a personal cost for skipping it: a
competition adductor injury he now manages with a weekly stretch, and an admitted years-long habit
of skipping post-workout stretching that he says he's still making up for.

---

**Q: What's the difference between the Beginner, Intermediate, and Advanced calendars?**

Same seven DVDs, same equipment, same midpoint cardio increase across all three. What actually
differs: Beginner has two extra rest days (10 total vs. 8) that the other two tiers don't
schedule; Intermediate introduces the harder DVDs (Full Body Strength and Conditioning, Explosive
Power Training) earlier and more often than Beginner; Advanced is the only tier that schedules two
full workouts on the same day (one AM, one PM), which is the real structural difference between
it and Intermediate. See `rushfit-beginner-training-calendar`, `-intermediate-`, and `-advanced-`
for the specifics.

---

**Q: How many calories should I be eating to lose weight on this program?**

The corpus gives a calculation, not a fixed number: your Basal Metabolic Rate (from
`rushfit-nutrition-guide`'s height/weight/age/gender formula) multiplied by an activity factor
tied to how many days a week you train (×1.2 for 1-2x, ×1.4 for 2-4x, ×1.6 for 4-6x), then a
deficit below that number. The guide names a floor: never go below 1,200 calories/day, and a
healthy pace of 1-2 lbs/week — eating too little is stated to backfire by triggering fat storage
rather than helping.

---

**Q: Is it okay if one side of my body is noticeably weaker or less coordinated than the other?**

Yes — this is stated as a normal, expected asymmetry across at least three independent sources
(`balance-and-agility`, `stretch-for-flexibility`, `strength-and-endurance`), not something to
correct before continuing. `strength-and-endurance` even gives a specific reason: "your brain is
not used to work equally both sides."

---

**Q: Does this corpus say anything about supplements, or specific medical conditions?**

No. This is a gap worth naming plainly rather than filling from outside knowledge: nothing in
this library discusses supplements, and the only medical guidance anywhere in the corpus is a
repeated instruction to consult a physician before starting (`rushfit-workout-guide`) and a
warning against training through pain (stated identically across several notes). Anything beyond
that is outside what this corpus covers.

sections.heading: 10 — Custom GPT Instructions
sections.intro:
This file is both the configuration for **Polymer Physical Fitness** and the record of how it is
meant to behave. The section marked **SYSTEM INSTRUCTIONS** can be pasted directly into the
Custom GPT's instructions field — it is the same content as `PASTE_INTO_GPT_INSTRUCTIONS.txt` at
the library root, lightly expanded here with headings and a file map for readability.

---

sections.heading: SYSTEM INSTRUCTIONS
sections.intro:
You are **Polymer Physical Fitness**, an interface built from the Georges St-Pierre RUSHFIT home
training program — nine workout DVDs (transcribed locally with Whisper; none were ever captioned
or posted to YouTube) and five program guides (Workout Guide, Nutrition Guide, and three 8-week
training calendars). **Treat the uploaded files as your working knowledge base, not a general
fitness textbook.**

subsections.body:
This is one complete home-fitness program, not a survey of fitness science. It has **no cited
studies anywhere** — every claim is the program's own coaching rationale or GSP's personal
account, and should be presented that way, not upgraded into settled science. This library is
architecturally ready to hold other home-fitness programs later (see each note's `program`
facet), but only RUSHFIT exists in it today.
subsections.heading: What this corpus actually is

subsections.body:
You are a coaching-technique and program-navigation interface, not a workout generator. Answer
from what a specific DVD or guide actually says; when a user describes a fault or a feeling ("my
knees cave in," "I can't finish the burpees"), route to the matching form cue or modification the
corpus names, rather than inventing generic fitness advice.

1. **Technique questions** ("how do I do X correctly," "what's the fault here") route to the note
   that teaches that movement in depth — `foundation-moves` for the base bodyweight/dumbbell
   movements, `the-fight-conditioning-workout` for striking/kick/grappling technique.
2. **Program-navigation questions** ("which calendar should I use," "when does X DVD come in")
   route to the three calendar notes and `rushfit-workout-guide`.
3. **Nutrition questions** route to `rushfit-nutrition-guide` specifically — do not blend in
   outside nutrition science.
4. **"Is this normal / should this hurt" questions** route to
   `04_SIGNALS_AND_SELF_ASSESSMENT.md` first, since this corpus draws a consistent, explicit line
   between acceptable fatigue/imperfect form and pain, which is never acceptable.
subsections.heading: Core interaction model

subsections.body:
Cite the specific note ID behind each claim (e.g. `foundation-moves`, `rushfit-nutrition-guide`),
resolving against `09_SOURCE_CATALOG.md`. Never present a claim as sourced if you can't trace it
to a note.
subsections.heading: Citations

subsections.body:
This program consistently offers named, sanctioned modifications for nearly every movement
(kneeling variants, shortened range of motion, substituted easier versions) — present these as
equally legitimate options, not lesser fallbacks, matching how the sources themselves frame them.
When GSP names his own weakness or limitation (endurance/isometric work vs. his explosive
strength; specific flexibility gaps), preserve that as his stated self-assessment, not as a
universal claim about all users.
subsections.heading: Preserve the source's own hedges and modifications

subsections.body:
- Never give medical advice beyond "consult your physician before beginning" and "never train
  through pain" — both stated directly and repeatedly in the corpus itself.
- Never invent exercise-science justifications, cited studies, or numeric thresholds this corpus
  doesn't state. If a mechanism is asserted (e.g. the stretch-shortening cycle, core as a
  "bridge" for striking power), attribute it as the program's own explanation, not as external
  biomechanics literature.
- Never treat GSP's personal reference scores (RUSHFIT Assessment, dumbbell weights he uses) as a
  target a user must hit — the corpus itself frames them as a comparison point, explicitly
  anticipating and normalizing a lower first attempt.
- Don't blend the three training calendars into one generic recommendation — their actual
  structural differences (rest-day count, DVD-introduction timing, same-day double sessions)
  matter and are specific to each tier.
subsections.heading: Boundaries

subsections.body:
A specific movement/technique question routes to `02_MOVEMENTS_AND_TECHNIQUE.md` plus the note
that teaches it in depth. A "which workout when" question routes to
`03_PRACTICES_AND_PROTOCOLS.md` and the three calendar notes. A "is this okay" question routes to
`04_SIGNALS_AND_SELF_ASSESSMENT.md`. A "why does the program do it this way" question routes to
`01_CORE_PRINCIPLES.md`. When the knowledge base doesn't cover something (supplements, injury
rehab, other training programs), say so directly and don't fill the gap with outside fitness
knowledge.

about_paragraphs: A reference built from {videos} sources across home fitness training programs — starting with Georges St-Pierre's RUSHFIT camp (nine DVD workout sessions and five program guides, designed by GSP and trainer Erik Owings) — synthesised into {library_files} knowledge files and {glossary_terms} glossary terms.

Every claim traces to a specific point in a specific source — a page in a guide, or a timestamp in a workout video. Nothing here is generated: there is no model in this app, and it makes no network requests. It works offline, permanently.

sections.body:
**"Core" is explicitly redefined at the outset to mean the whole stabilizing system, not just
visible abdominal muscles** — the workout is built to hit all of it across five rounds of
increasing difficulty: `[12:27]` "Don't think of only abdominals. Recognize that we're also using
our back extensors, our obliques, transverse abdominals, our rectus abdominals... we're using all
of these muscles." GSP frames the functional payoff directly in terms of striking power transfer:
`[37:01]` "The energy is transferred from the ball of my heel to my knuckle. If I have a good core
strength, I have less waste of energy... It's like the bridge between the two."
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
The same shared warm-up sequence as `balance-and-agility`, `stretch-for-flexibility`,
`the-fight-conditioning-workout`, and `full-body-strength-and-conditioning` — identical cues and
the same "body is like an elastic" framing `[02:12]`.
sections.heading: The Rush Fit Warmup (01:08–12:27)

sections.body:
| Round | Content | Distinguishing note |
|---|---|---|
| **1** `[13:28]`–`[18:34]` | One-leg dumbbell squat (30s/side) → dumbbell uppercut rotation → weighted overhead sit-up (1 min) → lying rotation → bicycle (1 min) | "Strength not only comes from the bicep, it comes from the hips." `[00:00]`, `[14:28]` |
| **2** `[18:34]`–`[24:42]` | Dumbbell swing (1 min) → dumbbell wood chop, both directions → repeat swing on the other hand → wood chop other direction → prone one-arm side press, both sides | Alignment cue: "imagine your chin's going through your belly button in a straight line" `[19:35]` |
| **3** `[24:42]`–`[30:53]` | Bodyweight circuit run twice through: power sit-up → single-leg glute bridge (right) → leg raise → single-leg glute bridge (left) → V-up | Framed as deliberate recovery before the hardest two rounds: "it's nice to get the body a little break because rounds four and five are very difficult" `[24:42]` |
| **4** `[30:53]`–`[38:02]` | Opposites drill (all-fours, alternating opposite arm/leg, 5s holds, 2 min) → lateral plank with alternating hip lifts (2 min) → straight-up sit-up | "Don't let the static nature of this round fool you. This is very difficult." `[30:53]` |
| **5** `[38:02]`–`[44:18]` | Back bend (bridge on the balls of the feet, 30s) → navasana-to-sit-through combo → mountain climbers, run twice through | Named directly as the hardest round in the DVD: "this next one's going to be the most difficult" `[36:00]` |

Round 3's power sit-up is cued with an explosive, momentum-driven technique rather than a slow
grind: `[24:42]` "I'm not going slow. I'm trying to... like I'm throwing a ball in front of me."
Round 5's sit-through offers three stacked regressions for the same movement — a hand-boost, a
hip-swing-around variant, and a bent-knee variant — explicitly so "everybody can do" some version
of it `[42:16]`.
sections.heading: The five rounds (13:28–44:18)

sections.body:
The same hip flexor, butterfly/straddle, seated hamstring, hip-extensor rotation, quadruped lat,
and kneeling chest/delt stretch sequence as `the-fight-conditioning-workout`,
`full-body-strength-and-conditioning`, and `bonus-workouts`, including the identical "changing my
mind" closing framing `[52:25]`.
sections.heading: Cool-down (44:18–53:27)

sections.body:
As in `full-body-strength-and-conditioning`, this DVD closes with the entire `foundation-moves`
DVD run again in full — same squat, lunge, push-up, sit-up, back extension, rotation, core
activation, burpee, and all six dumbbell-movement segments, word for word. See that note for the
complete technique breakdown.
sections.heading: Foundation Moves, repeated in full (53:27–1:40:50)

sections.body:
- **Hip sag during the lateral plank is named as the specific symptom of core fatigue to fight,
  not accept**: `[34:56]` "The hips have a tendency when they dip here. We don't want them to
  dip."
- **Body tilt during the opposites drill is explicitly diagnosed as core fatigue, not a balance
  problem to fix separately**: `[31:55]` "there are tendencies... for their bodies to tilt.
  That's because their cores are fatigued."
- **A too-narrow base is named as the specific cause of collapse** during the opposites drill,
  with a direct fix: `[32:56]` "you need to do a wider base, that's why you're collapsing."
- **Cramping in the hamstrings/glutes during the single-leg glute bridge is named as a personal,
  expected response**, not a warning sign to stop entirely: `[25:44]` "I tend to even cramp a
  little here. So if that's the case, you can come up and lower down."
sections.heading: Form cues and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **The opposites drill** — an all-fours or kneeling stability hold, alternating the opposite arm
  and leg raised together, held 5 seconds per side `[30:53]`.
- **Navasana** — the boat-pose hold (straight or bent legs, chest up) used as the base position for
  round 5's sit-through combination; named directly using its yoga term `[38:02]`.
- **Sit-through** — a floor-to-standing transition passing through a Hindu-push-up-like position,
  with hand-boost, hip-swing, and bent-knee regressions offered `[39:02]`.
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body:
- **"It's like the bridge between the two"** — GSP's own description of core strength connecting
  leg-drive energy to striking power, "from the ball of my heel to my knuckle" `[37:01]`.
- **"Imagine your chin's going through your belly button in a straight line"** — the alignment cue
  for both the dumbbell swing and wood chop `[19:35]`, `[20:36]`.
- **"That's when you separate the adult from the kids right here"** — GSP's framing of the final
  push in round 4's straight-up sit-up finisher `[36:00]`.
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
- **Difficulty is named directly rather than downplayed for the hardest rounds**: `[32:56]` "This
  shouldn't be easy. It shouldn't be easy for anybody," and `[37:01]` GSP admits "I'm having a hard
  time standing up right now."
- **A scaled/kneeling variation is explicitly framed as equally legitimate**, not a lesser
  fallback: `[32:56]` "she's getting the same effect, it's just a little bit less intensity.
  That's totally acceptable."
- **The round-4/5 framing of core training's value is stated as GSP's personal career rationale**,
  not a general claim applied to everyone: `[37:01]` "that's what I need to get to what I want to
  accomplish in my career."
- **The closing training philosophy is stated as a personal rule generalized outward, explicitly
  marked as such**: `[44:18]` "If you train harder, your fight will be easier... It's the same
  thing for everyone in life."
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**Duplicates `foundation-moves` in full**, and **shares its warm-up and cool-down verbatim** with
`balance-and-agility`, `stretch-for-flexibility`, `the-fight-conditioning-workout`,
`full-body-strength-and-conditioning`, and `bonus-workouts` — now confirmed across every video
notated so far except `foundation-moves` itself. **Extends `the-fight-conditioning-workout`'s and
`full-body-strength-and-conditioning`'s core-activation material** with a specific mechanistic
claim neither of those notes states as explicitly: core strength as the literal energy-transfer
link between ground-leg-drive and strike output, not merely a stabilizer.

sections.body:
**This is a body-weight-only circuit built specifically to train the stabilizer muscles used
standing on one leg and changing direction quickly — muscles the source says ordinary life doesn't
touch — repeated for two full rounds with no weights required.** `[11:28]` "There's no weights
required. It's basically moving our body, and you're going to notice that there's a lot of
stabilizations going up on one leg throughout." The stated reason this matters beyond balance
drills in the abstract: `[16:40]` "If you notice in most functional activities, including
fighting, we spend a lot of time on one leg... Most of these muscles, they're asleep for a normal
human being in modern days."
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
Erik Owings leads a body-weight warm-up he describes as `[00:00]` "multi-faceted... allows you to
work every muscle of your body in a functional manner to get you ready for the work to come."
Sequence, each move run roughly 60 seconds:

| Move | Cue |
|---|---|
| **Torso twist** `[00:00]` | Elbows at shoulder height, rotate on a fixed pivot point — "imagine... a sphere... I don't want to go all the way around" |
| **Side bend** `[01:00]` | Kick the hip out and reach, keep knee-hip-shoulder stacked — "we don't want to bend forward... we want to keep our body stacked" |
| **Plank walk-out** `[02:04]` | Walk hands out to plank, then feet up to hands; bent-knee modification available for limited hamstring flexibility `[03:05]` |
| **Ginga** `[03:05]`–`[04:10]` | A Capoeira base step, described as "like a backward lunge" done side to side with a raised guard hand |
| **Walk-out push-up** `[04:10]`–`[05:12]` | Squat down, walk hands out to a full push-up, chest to the deck, stand only once the heels are back down |
| **Lateral lunge** `[05:12]` | Feet on "parallel lines," trail leg stays straight, arms counterbalance |
| **Push-up with lateral hold** `[06:14]`–`[07:14]` | Walk out, rotate into a side plank, hold (5s baseline, extendable to 30s), hips must not sag |
| **Air squat** `[07:14]`–`[08:17]` | Thighs to parallel, weight back through the heels, "knees initiate the motion, but then they start to sit back and down" |
| **Quadruped opposite knee-to-elbow** `[08:17]`–`[09:21]` | Hands under shoulders, knees under hips, extend and hold, same side repeated before switching |
| **Lying sit-up** `[09:21]`–`[10:25]` | Toes pulled back, hands overhead, sit straight up to touch the ceiling |

Erik's framing of the warm-up's purpose: `[10:25]` "This is not a race... The importance of this
is the form, and it's not the repetition... to be able to break a little bit of sweat and ready to
go... for a hard workout." `[01:00]` gives the warm-up's own rationale for going slow first: "The
body is like an elastic, if you try to stress an elastic when it's cold it's going to snap."
sections.heading: The Rush Fit Warmup (00:00–11:28)

sections.body:
A single dumbbell is set on the floor as a touch/reach marker (not lifted) for several moves.
Erik states the design intent directly at the top: `[13:35]` "That's a consistent theme
throughout... whenever you do a lateral lunge, we don't want our toes pointing out or in." The
circuit runs once, then repeats from the gorilla squat `[30:46]`:

| Move | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Four-way lunge** `[11:28]` | Rotate right, lunge left leg, touch down with right hand; then mirror — always returning to center |
| **Lateral lunge** `[12:33]` | Side to side, "let your legs do the work," works "pretty much all the leg muscles" |
| **Backward lunge** `[12:33]`–`[13:35]` | Step back, touch down with same-side hand as the stepping leg |
| **Crossback lunge** `[13:35]` | Stand fully between reps, step behind, touch down same-side |
| **Single-leg dumbbell driver** `[13:35]`–`[15:39]` | Balance on one leg, reach to touch the dumbbell with the opposite hand, "part squat, part bend at the waist"; both sides |
| **Single-leg rotation reach** `[15:39]`–`[18:44]` | Step over, balance on one leg, reach/rotate across to touch the dumbbell, three variation angles from the same base position |
| **Airplane** `[18:44]`–`[19:50]` | Arms out wide, balance on one leg, rotate the torso side to side — Erik and GSP both name it as one of their own weaker moves |
| **X-hop** `[19:50]`–`[20:55]` | Jump feet in/out in an X pattern, 30 seconds |
| **Line hops** `[20:55]`–`[22:01]` | Quick feet side to side over a line, "soft bend in the knees... absorb the impact... in your muscles not in your joints" |
| **Gorilla squat** `[22:01]`–`[24:07]` | Fists to the floor, weight forward, hop feet to a full squat and stand, two reps one direction then rotate |
| **Mule kick (bullfrog drill)** `[24:07]`–`[25:12]` | Hands down, kick both legs up together, stand; a no-kick "just lift your legs" regression is offered |
| **Alligator crawl (bear crawl)** `[25:12]`–`[27:35]` | Elbow to knee, hips as low as possible, two steps forward/two back — "the lower you keep your hips... the more difficult it is" |
| **Floor pull-up with pop-up** `[27:35]`–`[28:39]` | Prone, pull on the elbows to arch and drag forward, pop up to standing, turn, repeat the other way |
| **Walking lateral push-up** `[28:39]`–`[30:46]` | Side to side, cross one hand over, push-up optional each rep — "over, under, out"; kneeling push-up or a no-push-up regression both offered |

Round two repeats gorilla squat → mule kick → alligator crawl → floor pull-up/pop-up → walking
lateral push-up `[30:46]`–`[35:59]`, run faster and against a countdown rather than a fresh
introduction of form.
sections.heading: The balance-and-agility circuit, two rounds (11:28–36:04)

sections.body:
After GSP taps out at the end of round two, he and Erik state the program's standard for
"perfect" performance directly, not as an aside: `[37:01]` **"If you could do this workout 100%
with the perfect form, perfect timing and everything, you do this workout perfectly. That's mean
this workout is not good enough for you... you need to go to another level."** GSP immediately
qualifies that this isn't a claim he himself meets: `[37:01]`–`[38:03]` "If I do the perfect form
and the perfect timing, I can't do this perfectly... I'm always looking for perfection. I'm always
going to get closer to the perfection, but... never reaching it." The distinction the co-host
draws for what's acceptable versus not: `[37:01]` not "picture perfect," but never to "the point
where he feels joint pain or pain with his body."
sections.heading: Design philosophy: "not good enough for you" (36:59–38:26)

sections.body:
- **Fatigue changing your form is the stop signal, not a rep count**: `[02:04]` "if you find
  you're starting to fatigue, the form is starting to go away, step back."
- **Breaking a sweat is the warm-up's target sensation**, not exhaustion: `[02:04]`, `[06:14]`
  "if you're finding you're out of breath and you're about to pass out, you probably need to slow
  down."
- **Gaze fixes balance**: `[14:36]` "if I look this way, I'll fall down a lot of times... you want
  to stay looking right at your target."
- **Collapsing form means shorten the range, not stop**: `[17:43]` "if you find you're collapsing
  every time, just shorten your range of motion."
- **A "burning" sensation location varies person to person** and is treated as normal: `[17:43]`
  "everybody's got a different spot that will start burning... their hips do."
- **Losing balance and stepping down is explicitly normalized**: `[15:39]`, `[19:50]` "if you lose
  your balance, just try to give a touchdown and get right back in the stance. That's natural and
  normal."
- **Hip height is the load dial on the alligator crawl**: `[26:17]`, `[32:52]` "the lower you keep
  your hips... the more difficult it is, the more they raise, the less resistance you have."
sections.heading: Form cues and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **Ginga** — a Capoeira base step, danced side to side with a raised guard hand; described here
  as a warm-up move resembling a backward lunge `[03:05]`.
- **Gorilla squat** — hands braced on the floor, weight forward, hop the feet up into a full squat
  and stand, repeated while walking forward then rotating `[22:01]`.
- **Mule kick** — also called a "bullfrog drill" by name in the source: hands braced on the floor,
  kick both legs up together, then stand `[24:07]`.
- **Alligator crawl** — also called a bear crawl; elbow-to-knee crawl kept as low to the floor as
  possible `[25:12]`.
- **Floor pull-up with pop-up** — prone, pull forward on the elbows arching the back, then push up
  to standing `[27:35]`.
- **Airplane** — balanced on one leg, arms out wide, rotating the torso side to side `[18:44]`.
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body:
- **"The body is like an elastic — stress it cold and it snaps; warm, you can stretch it"**
  `[01:00]`, as the stated reason to start the warm-up slow.
- **"Ultimate gym... ultimate workout"** — GSP and Erik's framing of the entire circuit needing no
  equipment: "just learning how to use your body the right way" `[35:59]`.
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
This is an instructional workout video, not a studied claim — its "evidence" is Erik Owings'
coaching rationale and GSP's own performance, not citations, and the source is explicit about the
limits of its own demonstration rather than presenting it as universal:

- **The design philosophy is stated as a moving target, not a pass/fail line**: `[37:01]`–`[38:03]`
  perfect execution is the goal precisely because it's framed as being always approached, never
  reached, even by GSP himself.
- **The safety line is drawn at pain, not at imperfect form**: `[37:01]` a rep done with "cheating"
  or "skipping" is acceptable; a rep that produces joint or body pain is not.
- **Individual variation is named repeatedly rather than smoothed over**: `[17:43]` "everybody's
  got a different spot that will start burning"; `[13:35]` "you always have one side better than
  the other."
- **The intensity/duration tradeoff is stated as the reason for this specific circuit's demands**:
  `[24:07]` "this is a shorter workout than our normal workouts. So you can sort of push it a
  little bit harder because... you're not doing it as long. [There's an] intensity and duration...
  inverse relationship there."
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
This is the first note written in the `physical-fitness` library, so there is nothing yet to
compare it against. Two things worth checking once more RUSHFIT sources are notated: whether the
"perfect form isn't the point, pain is the line" philosophy stated here at `[37:01]` is restated
or extended in the other workout DVDs (it is framed here as Erik and GSP's general coaching
stance, not specific to this session), and whether the Workout Guide PDF's equipment page —
which calls for "a small assortment of dumbbells" up to 25 lbs — reconciles with this workout's
use of a single dumbbell purely as a floor marker rather than a lifted weight.

sections.body:
**This is Body Beast's orientation module, not a workout — Sagi Kalev frames the entire 90-day
program before any exercise is shown, staking its results on three co-equal pillars (training
method, nutrition, and safety) rather than the workouts alone.** `[00:00]` "Body Beast is about
getting big, getting strong, getting a healthier approach to building muscle mass... I've taken the
best of old-school resistant training and fused it with the breakthrough in sports science we call
dynamic set training." He is explicit that effort alone is not the differentiator he's selling:
`[01:01]` "With my program, anyone can amaze their inner beast. But if you want that kind of
result... you have to be willing to do whatever it takes."
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
The named technique is a stack of set types, not one method: `[01:01]` "single sets, supersets,
drawing sets, progressive sets, drop sets, force sets, combo sets, and multi sets" — stated purpose
"pre-fatigued the muscle, activate more muscle fibers, and enhance the testosterone levels." The
plain-English translation he gives himself: `[01:01]` "if you feel yourself right, your body will
have no choice but get big."

Kalev draws the line on what counts as legitimate effort versus a shortcut: `[01:01]` "If any
exercise feels easy, you either need to lift more weights or to be more conscious of your form.
Sometimes people use bad form, momentum, or limited range of motion to lift more weights, not if
you want to be a beast."
sections.heading: Dynamic set training and effort standard (00:00–02:02)

sections.body:
Nutrition is stated as a precondition for results, not a complement to them: `[02:02]` "The most
important thing you can do is work correctly. The workouts are one thing, but if you are not
fueling yourself to add muscle, you won't get the results you want." The volume-of-food framing is
notably permissive on food choice, conditional on ratios: `[02:02]` "If you want to get huge, you
need to eat a lot. And it can be brownies, sundaes and pizza. You will have to eat the right foods
in the right macronutrient ratios." Supplementation is framed as a practical fix for a stated
difficulty (eating enough, consistently) rather than a separate claim of its own: `[02:02]`
"Anybody builder will tell you that one of the hardest thing to do is to eat all day long. One of
the easiest ways to do this is to supplement your diet."
sections.heading: Nutrition and supplementation (02:02–03:02)

sections.body:
Kalev orders the equipment list explicitly rather than treating it as a flat checklist: `[03:02]`
"Let's look at it in order of importance."

| Equipment | Stated role | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Dumbbells** `[03:02]` | Top of the list | Range used across the program "10 to 60 pound"; his own example spread: "15s from Reverse Flies, but 70s to do a Chest Press" |
| **Easy bar** `[03:02]`–`[04:03]` | "the central part of the body beast workout" | "target different muscle fibers and lift heavier weights that you might have available with dumbbells alone"; a dumbbells-only option exists for every workout, but "you will be happier if you invest" |
| **Resistance bands** `[04:03]` | Entry-level substitute | "providing resistance up to 100 pounds throughout the exercise"; also substitutes for pull-ups via a door attachment |
| **Weight bench or stability ball** `[04:03]`–`[05:06]` | Base for most exercises | The ball trades stability for instability training — "an even better workout for your stabilizers and core" — at the cost of safe load: "you will not be able to lift as much weight safely" if using it |
| **Chin-up bar / door attachment / Chin-Up Max** `[05:06]` | Pulling work | The Chin-Up Max is named as a bodyweight-assist device, not a bar substitute: "make a difference in finishing your required reps" |
| **Jump Mat** `[05:06]` | Joint/spine protection | "shock-resistant for your joints during jumping and support your spine during core work," called out specifically for Beast Cardio |
sections.heading: Equipment, ranked by importance (03:02–06:09)

sections.body:
The safety section is framed as a standing rule, not situational advice: `[06:09]` "the Beast's
number one rule, always be safe. Nobody gets big when they are nursing an injury." Medical
clearance is named first: `[06:09]` "If you have any medical conditions, including any kind of
sport or other injury, you should always speak with your doctor or physical therapist... based on
your individual situation of your personal limits."

Specific mechanical cues given, by equipment/movement:

- **Lifting from the ground**: `[07:11]` "bend your knees. Engage your abs and lift with your
  legs."
- **Lifting from the bench**: `[07:11]` "place a dumbbell on each knee and kick them up one at a
  time towards your shoulders."
- **Stability ball**: `[07:11]`, `[08:13]` pick up the weights before getting on the ball, "sitting
  on it first and then roll into position"; check dry clothing so "your torso, neck and shoulders
  are not slippery," and ball height fitted to the body.
- **Skull crushers** (easy bar or dumbbells): `[07:11]` "make sure you are completely in control of
  the weights... extremely cautious at any time you are bringing the weight, the bar, the band
  towards your face."
- **Easy bar**: `[08:13]` "make sure the safety clips are securely placed before lifting the bar."
- **General weight discipline**: `[08:13]` "always, always be conservative with the amount of
  weight you are lifting. There is plenty of time to become a beast. You don't have to max it out
  on the first day."

A non-lifting hazard is also named directly: `[06:09]` "More accidents happen in the gym by people
tripping over the equipment than any actual exercise-related incident. So pick up your stuff."
sections.heading: Safety rules (06:09–09:17)

sections.body:
Kalev directs viewers to an external support system rather than positioning the DVDs as
self-contained: `[09:17]` "The Team Beach Body Message Board and Super Gym have amazing tools to
help you achieve your goals... 24-hour support, coaches, access to others doing the beast, expert
[answers] to your fitness and nutrition questions, online scheduling and meal planning." The
Beachbody Challenge is framed around photographic evidence of progress, tied to specific days:
`[09:17]`–`[10:20]` "don't forget to take your photos on day 1, day 30, day 60 and day 90... those
photos are the only way you will be able to track your success and see your inner beast emerge."
sections.heading: Team Beachbody support and the Beachbody Challenge (09:17–10:55)

sections.body:
- **"Feels easy" is a signal to increase difficulty, not a pass**: `[01:01]` "If any exercise feels
  easy, you either need to lift more weights or to be more conscious of your form."
- **Instability trades against load**: `[04:03]`–`[05:06]` a stability ball increases demand on
  stabilizers and core but requires lighter weight to stay safe.
- **Face-directed weight requires full control, named as a distinct risk category**: `[07:11]`
  skull crushers specifically called out as a movement to be "extremely cautious" with.
- **Dry hands and dry equipment-contact surfaces are a stated safety precondition**: `[06:09]`,
  `[08:13]` "make sure your hands are dry before lifting any piece of equipment," and torso/neck/
  shoulders not slippery on the ball.
sections.heading: Form cues and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **Dynamic set training** — Kalev's name for combining multiple set types (single, super, drawing,
  progressive, drop, force, combo, multi) in one program to pre-fatigue muscle and recruit more
  fibers `[01:01]`.
- **Easy bar** — the source's own term (heard as "easy bar" in this transcript) for the EZ-curl-
  style bar central to the program's heavier lifts `[03:02]`.
- **Chin-Up Max** — a bodyweight-assist device used with a chin-up bar for lifters not yet able to
  do a full unassisted rep `[05:06]`.
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body:
- None stated as such in this source — the module is direct instruction and program philosophy
  rather than illustrative comparison.
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
This is a promotional/instructional program introduction, not a studied claim, and it is explicit
that results depend on adherence the source cannot enforce:

- **Nutrition is stated as a precondition, not an enhancer**: `[02:02]` "if you are not fueling
  yourself to add muscle, you won't get the results you want," with the guidebook's nutrition
  section framed as mandatory: "follow it like your results depend on it, because they do."
- **The effort bar is stated as self-assessed, not measured by the program**: `[01:01]` "you have
  to be willing to do whatever it takes" — the source has no way to verify this beyond the
  viewer's own honesty about form and load.
- **Individual load variation is named directly rather than given as a fixed number**: `[03:02]`
  "Everyone is different as is every muscle group... you will have to figure out what works for
  you," illustrated with Kalev's own mismatched personal numbers (15 lb reverse flies vs. 70 lb
  chest press).
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
This is the first Body Beast note written in the `physical-fitness` library alongside the existing
RUSHFIT sources, so there is no other Body Beast note yet to reconcile it against. One thing worth
checking once more Body Beast sessions are notated: whether the "conservative weight, don't max out
on day one" caution stated here at `[08:13]` is restated or contradicted by the intensity standard
in the individual workout videos (`beast-abs`, `beast-cardio`, and the `build-`/`bulk-`/`tempo-`
sessions). Against RUSHFIT: RUSHFIT's `balance-and-agility`[37:01] frames its safety line as "pain,
not imperfect form"; Body Beast's framing here is closer to "conservative load first," a different
emphasis (load discipline vs. form/pain) worth tracking as more Body Beast sessions are added.
